# On the Computational Hardness of Transformers

**Authors:** Barna Saha University of California San Diego bsaha@ucsd.edu Yinzhan Xu11footnotemark: 1 University of California San Diego xyzhan@ucsd.edu Christopher Ye11footnotemark: 1 University of California San Diego czye@ucsd.edu Hantao Yu Columbia University hantao.yu@columbia.edu Supported by NSF HDR TRIPODS Phase II grant 2217058 (EnCORE Institute).Supported by NSF grant CCF2008733, ONR grant N00014-22-1-2713, NSF Grant CCF-2238221 and a Columbia Center of Artificial Intelligence Technology grant.

## Abstract

The transformer architecture has revolutionized modern AI across language, vision, and beyond. It consists of $L$ layers of multi-head attention, where each layer runs $H$ attention heads in parallel and feeds the combined output to the subsequent layer. In attention, each token within an input of length $N$ is represented by an embedding vector of dimension $m$ . Computationally, an attention mechanism primarily involves multiplying three $N\times m$ matrices, while applying a softmax operation to the intermediate product of the first two matrices. A significant body of work has been devoted to analyzing the time complexity of attention, leading to several recent advances.

On the other hand, known algorithms for transformers compute each attention head independently. This raises a fundamental question that has recurred throughout theoretical computer science under the guise of “direct sum” problems: can multiple instances of the same problem be solved more efficiently than solving each instance separately? Many answers to this question, both positive and negative, have arisen in fields spanning communication complexity and algorithm design. Thus, a key challenge in understanding the computational hardness of transformers is to determine whether their computation can be performed more efficiently than $LH$ independent evaluations of attention.

In this paper, we resolve this question in the negative, and give the first non-trivial computational lower bounds for multi-head multi-layer transformers. In the small embedding regime ( $m=N^{o(1)}$ ), computing $LH$ attention heads separately takes $LHN^{2+o(1)}$ time. We establish that this is essentially optimal under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH). In the large embedding regime ( $m=N$ ), one can compute $LH$ attention heads separately using $LHN^{\omega+o(1)}$ arithmetic operations (plus exponents), where $\omega$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. We establish that this is optimal, by showing that $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}$ arithmetic operations are necessary when $\omega>2$ . Our lower bound in the large embedding regime relies on a novel application of the Baur-Strassen theorem, a powerful algorithmic tool underpinning the famous backpropagation algorithm.

## 1 Introduction

The Transformer architecture [VSP+17] is used for a wide range of tasks such as natural language processing [RWC+19] and computer vision [DBK+21, KMR+23], and has achieved state-of-the-art performance for numerous applications. The crucial building block of transformers is the attention head, which captures pairwise relationships between input tokens and thus is desirable for processing language inputs. Concretely, given input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ , the attention head consists of query, key and value embedding maps $Q,K,V:\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ , where $m$ is known as the embedding dimension, and computes

$$ \mathrm{Att}_{Q,K,V}(X)=\mathrm{softmax}(Q(X)K(X)^{\top})V(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}, $$

where the softmax operator is defined as

$$ \mathrm{softmax}(v)=\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\exp(v_{i})}\cdot(\exp(v_{1}),\ldots,\exp(v_{N})) $$

and is applied row-wise on matrices. A transformer consists of $L$ attention layers, where each attention layer consists of $H$ parallel attention heads that takes the output $X$ of the previous layer as input, sends it to all attention heads, and aggregate111Attention outputs can either be aggregated by sum or by concatenation. In Appendix C, we reduce summation aggregation to concatenation aggregation. Thus, we may consider summation aggregation without loss of generality. the outputs of all attention heads and $X$ before finally applying a row-wise multi-layer perceptron (MLP) function.

While the transformer is undoubtedly powerful, it is also computationally expensive, with attention complexity scaling quadratically with respect to input length $N$ . The trivial algorithm for attention requires $O(N^{2}m)$ time,222Following practical values, we always assume $m\leq O(N)$ . and the trivial algorithm for transformer requires $O(LHN^{2}m)$ time, even before accounting for the time required to compute embedding and MLP maps.333The time needed to compute MLPs eventually depends on its hidden dimension ${d_{\textup{hid}}}$ . For inputs in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , the time for computing MLP in practice should roughly be $O(m{d_{\textup{hid}}})$ . In this paper, we obtain lower bounds for transformers that do not have MLPs and whose embedding maps can be computed in linear time $O(Nm)$ . In Appendix B, we describe how to generalize our lower bounds to transformers with popular MLPs. Note that this only strengthens the lower bound, as these are specific instances of transformers. It has been proved that $N^{2-o(1)}$ time is necessary for computing attention when $m=\Omega(\log N)$ assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [KWH23, AS24], while the trivial algorithm of computing matrix products explicitly is optimal for all $m$ under a generalization of the OV Hypothesis [GHS+26]. Due to the lack of fast attention algorithms, numerous works have tried to address this bottleneck by proposing subquadratic alternatives to attention mechanism [KKL20, CLD+21, ZGD+20b, LYS+25]. However, all these subquadratic alternatives suffer from accuracy drops as the model scales up, and it has been proved that no subquadratic alternative can capture all pairwise relationship up to some approximation [AY25]. Consequently, our work is primarily concerned with the following question.

Question 1: How efficiently can a standard transformer model be computed?

While [KWH23, AS24, GHS+26] address this problem for a single attention head, we are instead concerned with transformers, which consist of many layers of multi-head attention. Proving lower bounds against transformers has been a critical challenge. Indeed, transformers appear to be significantly more complex than attention heads. Even while considering expressivity (i.e., which functions can be computed), there are relatively plentiful techniques to prove lower bounds against attention or single layer transformers (see e.g. one-way communication [SHT23] and split-VC dimension [KUJ+25]), but only a recent breakthrough established strong lower bounds against decoder-only transformers with many layers [CPW25].

Understanding the complexity of transformers is further motivated by known lower bounds on specific tasks that we hope transformers can handle. There are many simple, fundamental problems that require large transformers. For example, it is conjectured that any transformer that is capable of computing 3-SUM requires polynomial size (i.e. $mHL=N^{\Omega\left(1\right)}$ ) [SHT23, SHT24b]. Furthermore, shallow decoder transformers cannot compute function composition without polynomial width [CPW25]. If we nevertheless want to use transformers to compute such functions (e.g., 3-SUM naturally captures interactions between triples of input tokens), it is crucial that large transformers can be computed as efficiently as possible.

Beyond its obvious practical motivation, studying the complexity of transformers is also an interesting theoretical question on its own. Understanding the complexity of transformers is essentially understanding whether we can compute many attention heads faster than computing them one by one. One can ask such questions more generally:

Question 2: Can the cost of solving many copies of the same problem simultaneously be amortized more efficiently than solving each copy separately?

This is a recurring question in theoretical computer science, typically known as the “direct sum” problem, and there are numerous positive and negative examples to this question.

On the positive side, a famous result in communication complexity gives a partial function with complexity $\Theta(\log n)$ but constant $O(1)$ amortized complexity when computing many instances of the function at the same time [FKNN95]. Recently, a breakthrough obtained a similar result for total functions [MS25]. A degree $n$ polynomial can be evaluated on $n$ points in $\tilde{O}(n)$ time [Fid72] in contrast to the naive $\tilde{O}(n^{2})$ algorithm. Similarly, the product of an $n\times n$ matrix with $n$ distinct vectors can be computed in $O(n^{2.372})$ time [ADV+25] in contrast to $O(n^{3})$ which is required to compute them all separately. Moreover, to compute a transformer we do not need to compute each attention head explicitly. For example, the output of a layer is the sum of $H$ attention heads. For matrix products, given $n$ pairs of $n\times n$ matrices $\left\{A_{i},B_{i}\right\}$ , the sum of products, $\sum_{i}A_{i}B_{i}$ can be computed in $O(n^{3.251})$ time, much faster than computing each product separately, which takes $O(n^{3.372})$ time [ADV+25].

There is an equal abundance of results on the negative side. For example, monotone functions with independent inputs cannot be computed more efficiently than computing each separately [GF81]. Similarly, [Bsh89] give a direct sum theorem for certain classes of quadratic systems. [BB19] also obtain a strong direct sum theorem for randomized query complexity. [MWY13] use strong direct sum theorems to obtain distributed and streaming lower bounds for various sketching and estimation tasks. In contrast to the matrix-vector multiplication problem, it is widely hypothesized that the $(\min,+)$ -product of an $n\times n$ matrix with $n$ vectors cannot be computed in strongly subcubic time [VW18]. Question 2 falls naturally within this long line of research: asking whether transformers admit a direct sum theorem.

In this work, we essentially resolve Question 1 (or Question 2 in the case of attention and transformer) in the negative: we give the first non-trivial lower bounds for multi-head multi-layer transformer computation and show that the naive algorithm of computing each attention head separately is essentially optimal.

### 1.1 Our Contributions

We give stronger lower bounds for both the small embedding dimension ( $m=N^{o(1)}$ ) case and the large embedding dimension ( $m=N$ ) case. In the small embedding dimension case, the naive algorithm runs in $LHN^{2+o(1)}$ time while the previously known conditional lower bounds on attention [AS24, GHS+26] rule out algorithms in $LHN^{1-o(1)}+N^{2-o(1)}$ time. We show a significantly improved conditional lower bound, matching the naive algorithm.

#### Theorem 1.1 (Informal Theorem˜3.1).

Under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis or SETH, any algorithm computing $L$ layer, $H$ head transformers with summation aggregation and embedding dimension $m=\Omega\left(\log N\right)$ requires

$$ LHN^{2-o(1)} $$

time. The lower bound holds even if the transformer has no MLPs.

The $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis states that finding a triplet of orthogonal vectors among a set of $n$ vectors from $\{0,1\}^{\Theta(\log n)}$ requires $n^{3-o(1)}$ time. The $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis is a special case of the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, which has been used in many lower bounds e.g. [BRS+18, Li21, Bon22, ATYZ24, DLV25]. Furthermore, it is a consequence of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [Wil04], a strengthening of $\textbf{P}\neq\textbf{NP}$ and a popular conjecture in fine-grained complexity that states that there is no $2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}$ algorithm for satisfiability on $n$ variables [IP01] for any constant $\varepsilon>0$ . SETH implies essentially optimal lower bounds for problems including edit distance [BI15], graph diameter [RV13], dynamic programming problems [ATYZ24], approximate closest pair problems [ARW17], subset sum [ABHS19] and many other problems.

Even though many previous theoretical works model transformer embedding dimension to be roughly $O(\log N)$ , recent work also considers the scenario where embedding dimension is close to $O(n)$ . [YSBS+25] finds that for many practical graph datasets, the number of graphs (input length) could be well smaller than the embedding dimension of the transformers that are used in practice. For larger embedding dimension $m$ the bound in Theorem˜1.1 does not get better. For example, when the embedding dimension $m$ is the same as the input length (i.e. $m=N$ ), the best running time becomes worse: the naive upper bound is $O(LHN^{2}m)=O(LHN^{3})$ , and with fast matrix multiplication, the upper bound can be improved to $LHN^{\omega+o(1)}$ , where $\omega$ denotes the matrix multiplication exponent. An alternative lower bound can be obtained by using the existing conditional lower bound of $N^{\omega-o(1)}$ for a single attention computation [GHS+26]. Nevertheless, there remains a large gap between the best lower bound $\max\{LHN^{2-o(1)},N^{\omega-o(1)}\}$ and the best upper bound $LHN^{\omega+o(1)}$ , and the time complexity of transformer in this setting remains poorly understood.

In this work, we show that computing transformers is as hard as computing $\Theta(LH)$ instances of matrix multiplication, thus obtaining a matching $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}$ lower bound without any additional hypotheses, as long as $\omega>2$ .

Our result is shown in an extended version of the arithmetic circuit model, which is a generalization of the well-studied arithmetic circuit model (see e.g., [BCS13] for a book on arithmetic circuits). In the standard arithmetic circuit model, an algorithm only uses standard arithmetic operations $\left\{+,-,\times,/\right\}$ .

Since attention computation involves taking exponents, it is not clear how to compute attention at all using a standard arithmetic circuit, i.e. a standard arithmetic circuit cannot perform attention computation as simulating exponential function could already be hard enough. Thus, it is natural to also allow exponential gates and logarithmic gates in the arithmetic circuits we consider, and we call them extended arithmetic circuits (eACs). We remark that lower bounds against extended arithmetic circuits are stronger than lower bounds against arithmetic circuits, as any arithmetic circuit is an extended arithmetic circuit. Furthermore, all known algorithms for transformer computation exist in the extended arithmetic circuit model.

With fast matrix multiplication, it is easy to obtain an extended arithmetic circuit of size $LHN^{\omega+o(1)}$ that simulates $H$ -head $L$ -layer transformer inference with embedding dimension $N$ . We show that this is essentially optimal. In particular, any extended arithmetic circuit computing transformers requires size $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}$ .

#### Theorem 1.2 (Informal Theorem˜5.1).

Any extended arithmetic circuit computing $L$ -layer $H$ -head transformers with summation aggregation and embedding dimension $m=\Omega(N)$ has size at least

$$ LHN^{\omega-o(1)} $$

when $\omega>2$ . The lower bound holds even if the transformer has no MLPs.

We remark that when $\omega=2$ (i.e. transformers with $m=O(N)$ can be computed in $LHN^{2+o(1)}$ time), we can instead apply Theorem˜1.1 to obtain a matching $LHN^{2-o(1)}$ lower bound. For extension of our results to concatenation aggregation, see Appendix˜C.

Our lower bound on transformers shows that when embedding dimension is large, no significant improvement is possible outside fast matrix multiplication for computing transformers in the extended arithmetic circuit model. We provide a new way of proving lower bounds for multilayer transformer, which has been a challenging direction in this literature.

### 1.2 Technical Overview

In this section, we give an overview of our techniques.

#### Small Embedding Dimension.

We begin with our lower bound in the small embedding dimension regime $m=N^{o(1)}$ . Consider a $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance $A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\},B=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{N}\},C=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{LH}\}\subset\left\{0,1\right\}^{d}$ for some $d=\Theta(\log n)$ . Note that the three sets have different sizes, and we call it an unbalanced $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance. It is known that under the standard $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, such instances require $LHN^{2-o(1)}$ time. We construct a transformer $T_{C}$ with $L$ layers, $H$ heads per layer, and embedding dimension $O(d)$ such that $T_{C}(A,B)$ (with some simple postprocessing) determines whether $(A,B,C)$ contains an orthogonal triple. First, we specify the input to the transformer:

$$ X=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}^{\top}&b_{1}^{\top}&1\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
a_{N}^{\top}&b_{N}^{\top}&1\\
0_{1\times d}&0_{1\times d}&2\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

Except the last token, each token consists of one vector from $A$ , one vector from $B$ , and the constant $1$ . We now describe $T_{C}$ which has input dimension $2d+1$ . $T_{C}$ will consist of $L$ layers and $H$ heads per layer and embedding dimension $m=2d+2$ . For every head, we set $V$ to be $0$ in the first $2d+1$ columns, so that the output of the $\ell$ -th layer, denoted as $X^{(\ell)}$ , contains $X=X^{(0)}$ in the first $2d+1$ columns. In particular, we may assume that the input to every attention head contains $X$ in the first $2d+1$ columns.

We now describe the embedding map of each head. Since $|C|=LH$ , we can index $C=\left\{c_{h,\ell}\right\}$ and identify each vector in $C$ with one head in the transformer. Consider the $h$ -th head in the $\ell$ -th layer. We define embedding maps $q_{h,\ell},k_{h,\ell},v_{h,\ell}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ as follows. Note that since our maps do not depend on the $m$ -th coordinate, the following maps remain well defined for the first layer which is a map $\mathbb{R}^{m-1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ .

$$ \displaystyle q_{h,\ell} \displaystyle:u\mapsto-(u_{1},\dots,u_{d},0,\dots,0), \displaystyle k_{h,\ell} \displaystyle:u\mapsto(u_{d+1}\cdot c_{h,\ell}[1],\dots,u_{2d}\cdot c_{h,\ell}[d],0,\dots,0), \displaystyle v_{h,\ell} \displaystyle:u\mapsto(0,\dots,0,u_{2d+1})\text{.} $$

Note that we can implement the above maps with appropriate weight matrices $W_{Q,h,\ell},W_{K,h,\ell},W_{V,h,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ for all $h,\ell$ . Applying the above map to all $N$ tokens, we obtain

$$ Q_{h,\ell}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}-a_{1}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
-a_{N}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
0_{1\times d}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\end{pmatrix},\quad K_{h,\ell}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}b_{1}^{\top}\odot c_{h,\ell}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
b_{N}^{\top}\odot c_{h,\ell}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
0_{1\times d}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\end{pmatrix},\quad V_{h,\ell}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}0_{1\times(2d+1)}&1\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
0_{1\times(2d+1)}&1\\
0_{1\times(2d+1)}&2\end{pmatrix} $$

where $\odot$ denotes the entry-wise product of two vectors and $0_{a\times b}$ (resp. $1_{a\times b}$ ) denotes an $a\times b$ submatrix filled with constant $0$ (resp. $1$ ). Thus, the output of the $h$ -th head in the $\ell$ -th layer is $\mathrm{softmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)$ . To simplify the exposition slightly, we instead consider hardmax attention. The $\mathrm{hardmax}$ function maps a vector $v$ to a uniform distribution over its maximum elements. That is, for a vector $v$ with $I_{\max}(v)=\left\{i\mathrm{~s.t.~}v_{i}=\max_{j}v_{j}\right\}$ , $\mathrm{hardmax}(v)_{i}=\frac{1}{|I_{\max}(v)|}$ if $i\in I_{\max}(v)$ and $\mathrm{hardmax}(v)_{i}=0$ otherwise. A hardmax attention head then outputs $Z_{h,\ell}:=\mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)$ where $\mathrm{hardmax}$ is applied row-wise. It is known that hardmax attention can be approximated with softmax attention [SHT24b], so it is essentially without loss of generality to consider hardmax attention. In fact, by scaling the entries of $Q_{h,\ell}$ and $K_{h,\ell}$ by an appropriate factor on the order of $O(\log NHL)$ , we can ensure that each attention head outputs $Y_{h,\ell}$ such that

$$ \left\lVert Y_{h,\ell}-\mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)\right\rVert_{\infty}\ll\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(NHL)}\text{.} $$

Then, denoting $Z_{h,\ell}$ as the last column of $\mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)$ , we claim $Z_{h,\ell}$ is a vector whose $i$ -th entry is $2$ if $a_{i}$ and $c_{h,\ell}$ are not in any orthogonal triple (i.e. there are no $b_{j}$ such that $a_{i},b_{j},c_{h,\ell}$ are orthogonal) and at most $\frac{3}{2}$ if $a_{i},c_{h,\ell}$ participate in an orthogonal triple. This follows as in the former case, the set of maximum indices in the $i$ -th row is only $N+1$ where $V_{h,\ell}(X)$ contains a $2$ ; in the latter case, the set of maximum indices contains at least one other entry, and thus $\mathrm{hardmax}$ averages over at least one row where $V$ contains $1$ . Summing over all $h,\ell,i$ , we have $\sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i}Z_{h,\ell}[i]=2NHL$ if there is no orthogonal triple and at most $2NHL-\frac{1}{2}$ if there is. From (1), we can use $\sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]$ to determine if $A,B,C$ contains an orthogonal triple.

#### Large Embedding Dimension.

We now describe our lower bound for extended arithmetic circuits that compute transformers with large embedding dimension ( $m=N$ ). Recall that computing a single attention head is in $N^{\omega+o(1)}$ time, as we require two matrix products, one to compute $QK^{\top}$ and one to compute the product of $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top})$ and $V$ . It is then easy to see that we can use $O(LH)$ instances of matrix multiplication to compute a transformer with $L$ layers, $H$ heads, and embedding dimension $N$ .

The matching lower bound is much more challenging. While it is not too difficult to show that we can reduce matrix multiplication to a single attention head with embedding dimension $N$ (one can, for example, set $Q\leftarrow A$ , $K\leftarrow B^{\top}$ and $V\leftarrow I$ so that the attention head outputs $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top})$ . We can use a simple denormalization trick to obtain obtain $\exp(QK^{\top})$ instead (see Appendix˜A), from which we can compute $AB^{T}$ , it is not clear how to use a single transformer to simultaneously compute many independent instances of matrix multiplication. Consider as an example a transformer with a single layer and $H$ heads. The output of this transformer is the sum of all attention heads in this layer. As discussed earlier, the sum of matrix products can be computed more efficiently than computing each matrix product separately (e.g. the sum of $N$ matrix products can be computed in $O\left(N^{3.251}\right)$ time while computing each product separately requires $O\left(N^{3.372}\right)$ time. Thus, if we directly repeat the reduction of a single matrix product to a single attention head for all $LH$ heads in our transformer, the output of the transformer only computes the sum of $LH$ attention outputs, which has dimension $\Theta(N^{2})$ , in contrast to the $\Theta(LHN^{2})$ dimension required to express $LH$ distinct matrix products.

The key tool we require is the Baur-Strassen theorem [BS83], which was originally designed to show lower bounds in the arithmetic circuit model. Perhaps the most famous application of the Baur-Strassen theorem is the backpropagation algorithm, a fundamental building block of efficient training of neural networks [RHW86]. The Baur-Strassen theorem has also found applications in algorithm design [CGS15, Fis24]. We give a new application of the Baur-Strassen theorem: to obtain lower bounds for transformers. The Baur-Strassen theorem states that given an arithmetic circuit of size $s$ computing a function $f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , there is an arithmetic circuit of size $O(s)$ computing all the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to its $n$ inputs. In particular, Baur-Strassen gives us a powerful tool to extract more information from the partial computations within our algorithm, which provides an avenue to obtain the required $\Omega(LHN^{2})$ dimensional output.

In standard settings, an arithmetic circuit (Definition˜2.1) consists of $+,-,\times,/$ gates, and the size of a circuit is the total number of gates. As discussed previously, since the key non-linearity in attention is the softmax function which requires exponentiation, we equip our arithmetic circuits with $\exp$ and $\ln$ gates, and call them extended arithmetic circuits. Our first step is to give an extension of the Baur-Strassen theorem: if there is an extended arithmetic circuit of size $s$ computing a function $f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , then there is an extended arithmetic circuit of size $O(s)$ computing all the partial derivatives of $f$ .

Equipped with this tool, we now describe our lower bound construction. For simplicity, we describe our construction with what we call denormalized attention heads, which replaces the row-wise $\mathrm{softmax}$ with entry-wise $\exp$ . In particular, given $Q(X),K(X),V(X)$ , a denormalized attention head outputs $\exp(Q(X)K(X)^{\top})V(X)$ (see Appendix˜A for a more detailed discussion on denormalized attention heads). In the proof of Theorem˜1.2 (see Theorem˜5.1), we modify the construction given below to ensure that the matrix product can be extracted from a standard attention head (with normalization). Equipped with denormalized attention heads, we may construct a transformer $T$ that outputs a vector $T(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ with entries $T(X)_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp((A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})_{ij})$ where $A_{k},B_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ are arbitrary $N\times m$ matrices for $k\in[LH]$ . Our transformer simply consists of $H$ denormalized attention heads in each layer, where the $h$ -th head in the $\ell$ -th layer sets $Q_{h,\ell}(X)\leftarrow A_{(\ell-1)H+h}$ , $K_{h,\ell}(X)\leftarrow B_{(\ell-1)H+h}$ and $V_{h,\ell}(X)\leftarrow 1_{N\times 1}$ is the vector of all $1$ . (Technically $V_{h,\ell}(X)$ should be an $N\times m$ matrix, but here we do not need rest of the columns and can simply pad them with $0$ ’s.) Then, $\exp(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)=\exp(A_{(\ell-1)H+h}B_{(\ell-1)H+h}^{\top})\cdot 1_{N\times 1}$ is the vector consisting of row sums of $\exp(A_{(\ell-1)H+h}B_{(\ell-1)H+h}^{\top})$ . We then conclude by summing up the outputs of all heads in each layer, and proceed inductively across all $L$ layers.

Suppose there is an extended arithmetic circuit (eAC) of size $s$ that computes the transformer $T$ . We note that while our transformer $T$ has fixed embedding and MLP maps, and thus can be computed by a fixed circuit, the embedding and MLP maps may be parameterized by up to $O(m)$ weights which are additionally provided as input to the circuit. See Section˜2.2 for more detailed discussions on our models. Given the above transformer, our goal is now to apply the extended Baur-Strassen theorem to extract useful derivatives. We begin by modifying the input slightly. Introducing auxiliary input variables $C_{kij}$ for $k\in[LH]$ and $i,j\in[N]$ , we define $C_{k}$ to be the $N\times N$ matrix with entries $C_{k}[i,j]=C_{kij}$ . Then, we define for all $k\in[LH]$ matrices $\tilde{A}_{k},\tilde{B}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2N}$ where

$$ \tilde{A}_{k}=\begin{pmatrix}A_{k}&C_{k}\end{pmatrix},\quad\tilde{B}_{k}=\begin{pmatrix}B&I\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

First, we observe that $\tilde{A}_{k},\tilde{B}_{k}$ can be computed efficiently in $O\left(N^{2}\right)$ time.

We now describe how to use the transformer $T$ to compute the matrix product $A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}$ for all $k\in[LH]$ . Running the transformer $T$ and summing all entries of the output vector we obtain

$$ F\leftarrow\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\exp\left(\left(\tilde{A}_{k}\tilde{B}_{k}^{\top}\right)_{ij}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\exp\left(\left(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right)_{ij}+C_{kij}\right)\text{.} $$

Now, consider the derivative of $F$ with respect to $C_{kij}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial F}{\partial C_{kij}} \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial C_{kij}}\exp\left(\left(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right)_{ij}+C_{kij}\right) \displaystyle=\exp\left(\left(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right)_{ij}+C_{kij}\right)\text{.} $$

Now, if we set $C_{kij}\leftarrow 0$ for all $k\in[LH]$ and $i,j\in[N]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial F}{\partial C_{kij}} \displaystyle=\exp\left(\left(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right)_{ij}\right)\text{.} $$

Thus, by applying the extended Baur-Strassen theorem, we obtain the entries of $\exp\left(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right)$ . From, here, applying $O\left(LHN^{2}\right)$ $\ln$ gates, we obtain the desired $LH$ matrix products. In particular, we obtain an eAC of size $O\left(s+LHN^{2}\right)$ that computes $LH$ independent matrix products.

The final ingredient we require is a lower bound on the size of any eAC that computes $LH$ independent matrix products. While it is well-known that a standard arithmetic circuit requires $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}$ size to compute $LH$ independent matrix products (see Lemma˜4.5), the lower bound for extended arithmetic circuits is a bit more subtle. At first glance, an extended arithmetic circuit may be significantly more powerful than a standard arithmetic circuit, and may be able to compute matrix products using fewer than $N^{\omega}$ gates. We show that when restricted to low degree functions, any extended arithmetic circuit of size $s$ can be simulated by a standard arithmetic circuit (without $\exp$ and $\ln$ gates) of size $O(s)$ . That is, extended arithmetic circuits exhibit no advantage when computing low degree functions. Our result extends that of Strassen [Str73] (see [Blä13] for an exposition), which states that division gates are not useful for computing low degree functions, and may be of independent interest.

### 1.3 Further Related Work

We review two lines of work in the theoretical study of transformers: (1) the expressivity of transformers, i.e. what functions can transformers compute and learn; (2) complexity of transformers i.e. how efficiently can transformers (or approximations of transformers) be computed?

#### The Expressivity of Transformers.

There is a long line of work studying the expressivity of transformers. Several works, initiated by [HHG+20, YPPN21], establish the advantage of transformers over recurrent architectures in tasks such as parsing hierarchical structure [YPPN21], sparse averaging [SHT23], in context learning [WDL25], copying [JBKM24], and document similarity [AY25].

Despite their expressive power, lower bounds against transformers show that many functions cannot be computed with small transformers. Lower bounds against transformers typically rely on communication complexity [SHT23, PNP24, SHT24b] for depth one lower bounds, or reductions to other computational models [MS23, PNP24, SHT24b]. Notably, [SHT24b] connects the transformer model with the Massively Parallel Computation model by proving an equivalence between transformer and MPC protocol under certain parameters, and thus provide lower bounds on transformers using problems that are hard in MPC. In addition, a hard function for transformers with depth $\tilde{O}(1)$ was exhibited [CPW25]. [Hah20] establish that hardmax transformers cannot compute parity or dyck languages.

#### Algorithms and Hardness for Transformer Computation.

The exact computation of attention is fairly well understood, with quadratic lower bounds established in the small embedding regime [KWH23] and extended to more generic settings [AS24, AY25, GHS+26]. In light of these lower bounds, subquadratic algorithms have been developed in the special settings of small entries [AS24] and constant embedding dimension [GHS+26].

Given the hardness of exact attention computation, a long line of work has studied efficient approximations of attention, including [BMR+20], Reformer [KKL20], [KVPF20], Big Bird [ZGD+20a], Scatterbrain [CDW+21], Performer [CLD+21], KDEFormer [ZHDK23], HyperAttention [HJK+24], and Polysketchformer [KMZ24]. More recently, [YA25] provides a new direction of computing large input length transformers with smaller input length transformers.

Practical attempts at improving transformer performance typically turn towards hardware optimization, including techniques such as FlashAttention which optimizes I/O complexity [DFE+22, FEN+23, SY24] and speculative decoding which leverages parallelism [LKM23].

## 2 Preliminaries

Notations. Let $[n]$ denote the set $\left\{1,\dotsc,n\right\}$ . Let $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ denote the set of non-negative reals and $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ denote the set of positive reals. $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0},\mathbb{R}_{<0}$ are defined analogously. Our logarithmic function $\log$ is the base $2$ $\log$ unless otherwise specified.

For a ring $R$ , let $R[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}]$ denote the set of polynomials over $n$ variables with coefficients in $R$ , and let $R[[z]]=\{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n}|a_{n}\in R\}$ denote the set of formal power series over $z$ with coefficients in $R$ .

Let $e_{i}$ denote the $i$ -th basis vector with $0$ in every coordinate but $1$ in the $i$ -th coordinate. Let $I_{n}$ denote the identity matrix of dimension $n$ . For any matrix $A$ , denote the $(i,j)$ -th entry with $A_{ij}$ or $A[i,j]$ ; we typically use the latter if the matrix name itself has a subscript. Let $A[i;]$ denote the $i$ -th row of $A$ and $A[;j]$ the $j$ -th column of $A$ . For a vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , let $\mathrm{diag}(v)$ denote the $n\times n$ matrix with entries $\mathrm{diag}(v)_{ii}=v_{i}$ . For a matrix $A$ , let $A^{\top}$ denote its transpose and $A^{-1}$ its inverse. For any function $f$ , let $f(A)$ denote the matrix obtained by applying $f$ to each entry of $A$ . Similarly, let $A\leq B$ denote that $A_{ij}\leq B_{ij}$ for every entry of $A,B$ . Let $A\odot B$ denote the entry-wise product between two matrices. Let $0_{a\times b},1_{a\times b}$ denote the $a\times b$ matrix consisting of all zeros and all ones respectively. Let $I_{n}$ denote the $n\times n$ identity matrix.

The softmax operator is defined as

$$ \mathrm{softmax}(v)=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(v_{j})}\cdot(\exp(v_{1}),\dots,\exp(v_{N}))\in\mathbb{R}^{N} $$

for $v\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ . We also define the hardmax operator as

$$ \mathrm{hardmax}(v)[i]=\frac{\mathbf{1}\left[i\in I_{\max}(v)\right]}{|I_{\max}(v)|} $$

where $I_{\max}(v)=\left\{j:v_{j}=\max v\right\}$ . Given a matrix $A$ , we abuse notation and use $\mathrm{softmax}(A)$ and $\mathrm{hardmax}(A)$ to denote the matrix after we apply $\mathrm{softmax}$ and $\mathrm{hardmax}(A)$ , respectively, on each row of $A$ .

### 2.1 Arithmetic Circuits

#### Definition 2.1.

An arithmetic circuit (AC) is a sequence of operations $\left\{g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s}\right\}$ such that each $g_{j}\leftarrow y\circ z$ for $\circ\in\left\{+,-,\times,/\right\}$ and $y,z\in\left\{g_{i}\right\}_{i<j}\cup\left\{x_{i}\right\}\cup\mathbb{R}$ with a subset of gates $\left\{g_{i_{k}}\right\}$ denoted the output gates. Given input $x$ , denote $\mathcal{C}(x)$ as the values on the output gates. An arithmetic circuit $\mathcal{C}$ computes $F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ if $\mathcal{C}(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ .

The matrix multiplication exponent $\omega$ is defined as the smallest constant such that the product of two $n$ by $n$ matrices can be computed by an arithmetic circuit of size $O(n^{\omega+\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ .

We will also consider a more general class of circuits, which include exponential and logarithmic gates.

#### Definition 2.2.

An extended arithmetic circuit (eAC) computing $F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a sequence of operations $\left\{g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s}\right\}$ such that each $g_{j}$ is one of the following forms:

- 1. $g_{j}\leftarrow y\circ z$ for $\circ\in\left\{+,-,\times,/\right\}$ and $y,z\in\left\{g_{i}\right\}_{i<j}\cup\left\{x_{i}\right\}\cup\mathbb{R}$ .

- 2. $g_{j}\leftarrow\exp(y)$ for $y\in\left\{g_{i}\right\}_{i<j}\cup\left\{x_{i}\right\}\cup\mathbb{R}$ .

- 3. $g_{j}\leftarrow\ln(y)$ for $y\in\left\{g_{i}\right\}_{i<j}\cup\left\{x_{i}\right\}\cup\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ .

### 2.2 Transformers

We first define a self-attention head, the core primitive of a transformer. Let $N$ denote the context (input) length, $m$ the embedding (hidden) dimension, and ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ the input dimension. Recall that following practical values, we assume $m=O(N)$ . For an input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ , we refer to each row of $X$ as a token.

#### Definition 2.3 (Attention).

A self-attention head is a mapping $f_{Q,K,V}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ defined by

$$ f_{Q,K,V}(X)=\mathrm{softmax}(Q(X)K(X)^{\top})V(X) $$

and parameterized by row-wise query, key, and value embeddings $Q,K,V\colon\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ (e.g., $Q(X)=(Q(X_{1}),\dots,Q(X_{N}))$ . Let $\mathrm{Att}^{N}_{m,{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ denote the set of all self-attention heads with input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ , embedding dimension $m$ and input length $N$ . When $m={d_{\textup{in}}}$ , we denote this as $\mathrm{Att}^{N}_{m}$ .

Figure˜1 illustrates an attention head. In practice, and in our constructions, embedding functions typically take the form $Q(X)=XW_{Q}$ (analogously $K(X)=XW_{K},V(X)=XW_{V}$ ) for some weight matrices $W_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{{d_{\textup{in}}}\times m}$ .

Hardmax attention has also been widely studied in the literature [MSS22, SHT24b, JSLC25], especially in theoretical work. For each query, hardmax attention only allows it to attend to the keys that achieve the maximum inner product (highest correlation).

#### Definition 2.4 (Hardmax Attention).

A hardmax-attention head is a mapping $f^{\mathrm{hard}}_{Q,K,V}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ defined by

$$ f^{\mathrm{hard}}_{Q,K,V}(X)=\mathrm{hardmax}(Q(X)K(X)^{\top})V(X)\text{.} $$

In general, we use (self-)attention to mean softmax attention (Definition˜2.3) unless otherwise specified. Finally, we define the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), which is a shallow neural network. By the universal approximation theorem which states that any continuous function can be approximated by a MLP (with enough neurons), we model MLP as continuous functions on vectors.

#### Definition 2.5.

An MLP is a continuous function $\Psi:\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m_{2}}$ for $m_{1},m_{2}>0$ .

Given a matrix $A$ , we abuse notation and denote $\Psi(A)$ as the result of applying $\Psi$ row-wise on matrix $A$ . We now formally define transformers.

#### Definition 2.6 (Transformer).

A transformer is a mapping $T:\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{out}}}}$ specified by attention heads $\left\{f_{\ell,h}\right\}_{\ell,h=1}^{L,H}$ and element-wise MLP layers $\Psi_{\ell}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ for $\ell\in[L]$ . Upon input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ , the transformer computes intermediate embeddings $X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(L)}$ with

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\Psi_{\ell}\left(X^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{h=1}^{H}f_{\ell,h}\left(X^{(\ell-1)}\right)\right)~~~\forall\ell\in[L], $$

and returns $T(X)=\Psi_{O}(X^{(L)})$ for an output MLP $\Psi_{O}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{\textup{out}}}$ (let $X^{(0)}:=X$ for notational convenience).

A hardmax transformer is defined analogously, replacing each attention head with a hardmax-attention head.

Note that in this definition, we sum up the result of each attention head, which is considered in many theoretical works (e.g., [SHT23, SHT24b, SHT24a]). In the more standard version used in practice, the results of the attention heads are concatenated. In addition, in sum aggregation, the attention head dimension equals the embedding dimension $m$ , while in concatenation aggregation, the attention head dimension equals $m/H$ . As we can easily obtain the sum from the concatenation using a linear MLP, all our lower bounds can be adapted to the concatenation version. See Appendix˜C for details.

In this paper, we focus on attention mechanisms when proving hardness results, and show lower bounds for transformers without MLPs. In Appendix˜B, we show that our results hold also for transformers with standard MLPs found in practice, even when all MLPs take linear time to compute, i.e. given input $x\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , computing $\Psi(x)$ takes $O(m)$ time for MLP $\Psi$ . Finally, we are ready to define what it means for an algorithm to compute transformers.

#### Definition 2.7.

An algorithm computes transformers with context length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ and output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ if given any such transformer $T$ and any input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ , the algorithm outputs $T(X)$ .

For circuits, the definition is a bit more subtle. If we were to attempt to say a circuit $\mathcal{C}$ computes a transformer, then the circuit must be able to compute all possible embedding and MLP maps, then the circuit must encode many functions at once, which is too strong of a condition to require. Instead, we aim to give lower bounds against circuits meeting a much weaker requirement: we show lower bounds against circuits $\mathcal{C}$ that compute fixed transformers.

Although we consider fixed transformers, we remark that the embedding map may be parameterized. This corresponds in practice to the learned weights of a model. Formally, consider an attention head $f_{\ell,h}$ with embedding maps $Q_{h,\ell},K_{h,\ell},V_{h,\ell}$ . Then, we require that $(Q_{h,\ell})_{i}=g(w_{Q_{h,\ell}},X_{i})$ where $g$ is an function computable by an eAC, $w_{Q_{h,\ell}}$ denotes the weights associated to this map, and $X_{i}$ denotes the $i$ -th row of the input to the attention head. In our constructions, we require that $g$ is an eAC of size $O(m)$ . Let $W$ denote the concatenation of all the weights of the transformer, and for any eAC transformer $T$ , let $T_{W}(X)$ be the computation of $T$ with weights $W$ on input $X$ . Finally, we define what it means for a circuit to compute a transformer.

#### Definition 2.8.

Let $T$ be a transformer with context length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ and output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ . Suppose $T$ has weights $W$ and input $X$ . A circuit $\mathcal{C}$ computes $T$ if for any input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ and any weights $W$ , $\mathcal{C}(X,W)=T_{W}(X)$ .

To obtain meaningful lower bounds against small eAC computing transformers, we show that transformers can compute functions that are hard for extended arithmetic circuits. Of course, to have a meaningful lower bound, we note that the transformer itself must also be computable with an eAC.

#### Softmax Simulates Hardmax.

We introduce a useful primitive for Transformer computation and show that softmax attention can simulate hardmax attention when there is a sufficient gap between the maximum value and the second largest value. This is similar to a result of [SHT24b].

#### Lemma 2.9.

Let $f\in\mathrm{Att}^{N}_{m}$ be a self-attention unit with embedding functions $Q,K,V$ such that

- 1. $V(X)\in\left\{0,1,2\right\}^{n\times m}$ , and

- 2. for every $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ and $i\in[N]$ :

$$ A(X)_{i,i^{\prime}}\leq\max_{i^{\prime\prime}}A(X)_{i,i^{\prime\prime}}-1,\ \forall i^{\prime}\not\in I_{\max}(A(X)_{i}), $$

where $A(X)=Q(X)K(X)^{\top}$ .

Then there exists an attention unit $f^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Att}^{N}_{m}$ satisfying

$$ \left\lVert f^{\prime}(X)-\mathrm{hardmax}(A(X))V(X)\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)} $$

for an arbitrarily small inverse polynomial.

The idea behind the simulation is simple: by scaling each query vector in $Q$ by a sufficiently large constant $c=\Theta(\log N)$ , we ensure that any probability assigned to non-maximum indices by the softmax operation is exponentially small with respect to $c$ , i.e. less than $\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}$ for any polynomial. We leave the proof to Appendix˜A.

### 2.3 Fine-Grained Complexity

We state our major hypotheses in fine-grained complexity theory in this section. See Section˜1 for more discussions on their applications.

#### Hypothesis 2.10 (Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)).

For any $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $k\textup{-}\mathsf{SAT}$ requires $\Omega(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n})$ time, where $n$ is the number of variables in the CNF.

We say that $k$ vectors $v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in\left\{0,1\right\}^{d}$ are orthogonal if for all $j\in[d]$ , $v_{\ell}[j]=0$ for some $\ell\in[k]$ . In other words, their $k$ -wise inner product is $0$ . The $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ problem is then defined as follows: given $A_{1},\dots,A_{k}\subset\left\{0,1\right\}^{d}$ each of size $n$ , determine if there exists $v_{1}\in A_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in A_{k}$ such that $v_{1},\dots,v_{k}$ are orthogonal. The trivial algorithm of checking all $k$ -tuples of vectors requires $O(n^{k}d)$ time. The $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis states that for $d=\Theta(\log n)$ , this is essentially optimal: i.e. any algorithm requires $n^{k-o(1)}$ time.

#### Hypothesis 2.11 ( $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis).

Computing $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ on sets of $n$ vectors with dimension $\Theta(\log n)$ requires $n^{k-o(1)}$ time.

The $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis follows from the popular Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [IP01] which states that satisfiability over $n$ variables requires $2^{(1-o(1))n}$ time [Wil04]. Our lower bound is based on the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, a special case of $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ for $k=3$ .

The unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ problem is defined as follows: given $k$ sets of vectors $A_{1},\dots,A_{k}$ of size $S_{1},\dots,S_{k}$ , determine if there exist $v_{1}\in A_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in A_{k}$ such that $v_{1},\dots,v_{k}$ is orthogonal. The trivial algorithm of checking all $k$ -tuples requires $O(S_{1}S_{2}\dots S_{k}d)$ time. Again, the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis states that this is essentially optimal and it is well-known that the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis is equivalent to the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis.

#### Hypothesis 2.12 (Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis).

$k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ on sets $S_{1},\dots,S_{k}$ of size $n^{s_{1}},\dots,n^{s_{k}}$ with dimension $d=\Theta(\log n)$ requires $n^{s_{1}+\dots+s_{k}-o(1)}$ time.

It is clear that the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis implies the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, by setting $s_{1}=\dots=s_{k}=1$ . The following lemma shows the converse direction, and we include a proof in Appendix˜A for completeness.

#### Lemma 2.13.

Let $0<s_{2}\dotsc,s_{k}\leq 1$ . Let $A_{1},\dots A_{k}\subset\left\{0,1\right\}^{d}$ for $d=\Theta(\log n)$ with $|A_{1}|=n$ and $|A_{i}|=n^{s_{i}}$ for all $i>1$ . Then, any algorithm computing $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ on $A_{1},\dotsc,A_{k}$ requires time $n^{s_{1}+\dotsc+s_{k}-o(1)}$ under the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. In particular, the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis holds under the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis.

## 3 Lower Bounds for Small Embedding Dimension

We begin with lower bounds for the small embedding dimension setting (i.e. $m=N^{o(1)}$ ). Our lower bound is based on the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis (or SETH).

First, we show that under the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, when the embedding dimension is small (e.g. $m=\Theta(\log n)$ ), there is no algorithm that computes transformers significantly more efficiently than the naive algorithm that computes each head separately.

#### Theorem 3.1 (Formal Theorem˜1.1).

Let $m=\Theta(\log N)$ and $L,H=\mathrm{poly}(N)$ . Any algorithm computing transformers with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, and input and output dimension $m$ up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ requires $LHN^{2-o(1)}$ time under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. The lower bound holds even if the transformer has no MLPs.

In the above statement, we require $L,H=\mathrm{poly}(N)$ since in $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ the sizes of the three sets must be polynomially related. We remark that this is the interesting regime of the problem since when $L,H=N^{o(1)}$ , we obtain optimal lower bounds directly from the hardness of a single attention head.

#### Lemma 3.2.

Suppose there exists an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that computes any transformer with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $2d+2$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input and output dimension $2d+2$ , up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ in time $B$ , then there exists an algorithm that solves unbalanced $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ with dimension $d$ and size $N,N,LH$ in time $\tilde{O}(LHd+B)$ .

First, we observe that Theorem˜3.1 follows from Lemma˜3.2.

#### Proof of Theorem˜3.1 assuming Lemma˜3.2.

Suppose for contradiction that there is an algorithm computing any transformer with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m=2d+2$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input and output dimension $m$ up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ in time $O\left(LHN^{2-\varepsilon}\right)$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ . Then, consider an unbalanced $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance with dimension $d=\Theta(\log N)$ and size $N,N,LH$ . Lemma˜3.2 implies that there is a $\tilde{O}(LHd+LHN^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm for this problem, which contradicts the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. ∎

#### Claim 3.3.

For all $\ell$ , the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(\ell)}$ are the first $2d+1$ columns of $X$ .

#### Proof.

The claim follows as the first $2d+1$ columns of $V_{h,\ell}(X)$ are $0$ for all $h,\ell$ . As a result, the output of each head consists of $0$ in the first $2d+1$ columns. By induction, the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(\ell)}$ are the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(0)}=X$ . ∎

Secondly, we claim that the given hardmax transformer computes the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance. Notice that this suffices because of Lemma˜2.9, as an algorithm computing any softmax transformer can approximate any hardmax transformer with the same dimension. Consider the $(h,\ell)$ -th attention head. Note that

$$ (Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})_{i,j}=\begin{cases}0&\textup{if }\max(i,j)=N+1\\
-a_{i}\cdot b_{j}\cdot c_{h,\ell}&\textup{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

For $1\leq i\leq N$ , the maximum entry in the $i$ -th row is $0$ , since $(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})_{i,N+1}=0$ . Recalling that $I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})$ denotes the set of indices attaining maximum value in the $i$ -th row, we have that $|I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})|\geq 2$ if $(a_{i},c_{h,\ell})$ participate in an orthogonal triple and $|I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})|=1$ otherwise. In particular, let $t_{i}:=t_{i,(h,\ell)}$ denote the number of $j$ such that $a_{i}\cdot b_{j}\cdot c_{h,\ell}=0$ . Then we have

$$ \mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}0&\cdots&0&\frac{t_{1}+2}{t_{1}+1}\\
0&\cdots&0&\frac{t_{2}+2}{t_{2}+1}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&\cdots&0&\frac{t_{N}+2}{t_{N}+1}\\
0&\cdots&0&\frac{N+2}{N+1}\end{pmatrix} $$

In particular, for every $i\leq N$ , the $i$ -th entry in the last column is $2$ if $t_{i}=0$ and at most $\frac{3}{2}$ otherwise. Lemma˜2.9 then implies that there is a transformer such that each attention head computes an output $Y_{h,\ell}$ that approximates the hardmax attention head with embeddings $Q_{h,\ell},K_{h,\ell},V_{h,\ell}$ well. In particular, the output of the $h$ -th head in the $\ell$ -th layer, denoted $Y_{h,\ell}$ , satisfies

$$ \left\lVert Y_{h,\ell}-\mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{10NHL} $$

for some inverse polynomial in $L,H,N$ .

Let $Z_{h,\ell}$ denote the last column of $\mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)$ . If the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance is a no-instance (i.e. there is no orthogonal triple), then every $Z_{h,\ell}[i]=2$ , i.e.

$$ \sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{h,\ell}[i]=2NHL\text{.} $$

On the other hand, if the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ is a yes-instance (i.e. there is an orthogonal triple), then there exists some $i,(h,\ell)$ where $Z_{h,\ell}[i]\leq\frac{3}{2}$ i.e.

$$ \sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{h,\ell}[i]\leq 2NHL-\frac{1}{2}\text{.} $$

Let us then consider the output $X^{(L)}$ , in particular focusing on the last column, since the first $2d+1$ columns are exactly those of $X=X^{(0)}$ by ˜3.3. Observe that our transformer outputs for all $1\leq i\leq N$

$$ X^{(L)}[i,m]=X^{(0)}[i,m]+\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]=\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]\text{.} $$

Since our algorithm computes the given transformer up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ , we in fact obtain in the last column a vector $\hat{X}$ such that $|\hat{X}_{j}-X^{(L)}[i,m]|\leq\frac{1}{10N}$ for all $i\in[N]$ .

Thus, from the computed output of the transformer, we can compute in $O(N)$ time $\sum_{j=1}^{N}\hat{X}[j]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{X}[i]-\sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{h,\ell}[i]\right| \displaystyle\leq\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{X}[i]-\sum_{i=1}^{N}X^{(L)}[i,m]\right| \displaystyle\quad\quad+\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}X^{(L)}[i,m]-\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]\right| \displaystyle\quad\quad+\left|\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]-\sum_{h,\ell}Z_{h,\ell}[i]\right| \displaystyle\leq 0.2\text{.} $$

Here, we apply the triangle inequality, apply the approximation error of our algorithm for the first term, our equation above for the second term and (2) for the third term. Note that from the output of the transformer is a $(N+1)\times m$ matrix, but we sum only the first $N$ entries of the last column.

Thus, the sum $\sum_{j=1}^{N}\hat{X}[j]$ is at least $2NHL-0.2$ if there is no orthogonal triple and at most $2NHL-0.3$ otherwise. Therefore, we can compute the output of the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance.

∎

We conclude with a simple conditional lower bound which suggests that efficient transformers require large size to compute $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ , suggesting that small size transformers cannot handle some instances of $3$ -wise interaction.

#### Theorem 3.4.

Under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, any transformer with linear time embedding and MLP maps computing $d$ -dimensional $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ requires $LHm=N^{1-o(1)}$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose there is a transformer $T$ with embedding dimension $m=\Theta(\log N)$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension $m$ , output dimension $m$ that computes $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ with dimension $m$ . Recall that in an efficient transformer, all embedding and MLP maps require $\tilde{O}(m)$ time, so that each attention head is computed in $O(Nm+N^{2}m)=O(N^{2}m)$ time. Following the standard algorithm, this transformer can be computed in time $\tilde{O}(N^{2}mHL)$ . In particular, under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, this requires $LHm=N^{1-o(1)}$ . ∎

## 4 Tools for Algebraic Circuits

In this section, we establish some tools for (extended) arithmetic circuits which will be used in our lower bound proofs for large embedding dimensions.

While eAC is a more powerful class in general (e.g. AC cannot compute $\exp(x)$ ), we show that the additional gates are not necessary for computing matrix multiplication. More generally, we argue that we can in fact use standard arithmetic circuits to simulate an eAC that computes low degree functions. For our application, we give the result for quadratic functions. The proof generalizes that of [Str73] which states that division gates are unnecessary for quadratic functions.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Let $F=\{F_{1},\dotsc,F_{m}\}$ where $F_{i}=\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}t_{ik\ell}x_{k}x_{\ell}$ . Suppose there is an eAC $\mathcal{C}$ of size $s$ computing $F$ . Then there is an AC of size $O(s)$ computing $F$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an optimal eAC for computing $F$ , and let $W=(w_{1},\dotsc,w_{s})$ be an ordering of all gates in $\mathcal{C}$ where earlier gates are computed first. Without loss of generality, viewing each $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})$ as a function, we can assume $w_{i}\neq 0$ for any $i$ . Furthermore, since $\mathcal{C}$ computes $F$ for all inputs $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , $\mathcal{C}$ is well defined for all $x$ . In particular, if $w_{i}$ is ever provided as input to a $\ln$ gate, we have that $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})>0$ for all $x$ . Similarly, if $w_{i}$ is ever provided as a denominator to a $/$ gate, we have that $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\neq 0$ for all $x$ . By substituting $\tilde{x}_{i}\leftarrow x_{i}z$ , we can view each gate $w_{j}$ as a formal power series $\tilde{w}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})[[z]]$ with coefficients that are functions on $x_{1},\dots,x_{n}$ . We can do this as all the formal power series are well-defined when $\mathcal{C}$ is well-defined under all the inputs $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . First, the sum, difference, and product are well defined for any two formal power series, and exponentiation of a formal power series is well-defined (we will show the exact formulation later). For a function $f$ corresponding to some gate, and its formal power series $\tilde{f}$ , observe that $\ln(\tilde{f})$ is well defined as long as $\tilde{f}$ has positive constant coefficient (see exact formulation later). The constant coefficient of $\tilde{f}$ is $f(0,\dots,0)$ , and our assumption that inputs to $\ln$ gates are positive on all inputs ensures that $f(0,\dots,0)>0$ , which implies the constant coefficient of $\tilde{f}$ as needed. For a division gate $w_{j}=g/h$ , our assumption that any gate input to the denominator of a division gates is non-zero for all inputs ensures that the constant coefficient of $\tilde{h}$ is $h(0,\dots,0)\neq 0$ . The following fact then guarantees that the formal power series of $w_{j}$ is well defined.

#### Fact 4.2.

Let $R$ be a ring. A power series $\tilde{h}(z)=\sum_{i}a_{i}z^{i}\in R[[z]]$ is invertible if and only if $a_{0}\neq 0$ . Furthermore, the inverse is given by

$$ \frac{1}{\tilde{h}(z)}=\frac{1}{a_{0}}\left(1+q+q^{2}+q^{3}+\dotsc\right) $$

where $q=-\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_{i}}{a_{0}}z^{i}$ .

Viewing the gates as formal power series, we argue that the desired output can easily be computed from the low order coefficients of the power series of the relevant gates. Specifically, since all $F_{i}$ have degree at most $2$ , we can add a new variable $z$ to all the input $x_{i}$ and only look at the coefficients for $z^{0},z^{1},z^{2}$ . Suppose $w_{j}$ is an output gate $F_{i}$ . Then, we have

$$ F_{i}=w_{j}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}t_{ik\ell}x_{k}x_{\ell}\text{.} $$

Notice that

$$ w_{j}(x_{1}z,\dots,x_{n}z)=\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}t_{ik\ell}x_{k}x_{\ell}z^{2}\text{,} $$

whose formal power series is simply itself. Hence, we can compute $F_{i}$ from the coefficient of $z^{2}$ in the formal power series $\tilde{w}_{j}$ .

We have shown that from the second coefficient of the power series corresponding to the output gates we can compute $F$ efficiently. While we will not be able to compute the full power series of each gate as there could be infinitely many terms, we describe how to compute the low-order coefficients, i.e. the coefficients of $1,z,z^{2}$ , for all $\tilde{w}_{i}$ . We proceed by induction. We denote $\tilde{w}_{i}=\sum_{j\geq 0}c_{j}z^{j}$ and compute $c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}$ . For the input gates, $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=x_{j}$ for some $x_{j}$ so that $\tilde{w}_{i}=x_{j}z$ . In particular, $c_{0}=c_{2}=0$ and $c_{1}=x_{j}$ . This requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 1: Addition and Subtraction. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\tilde{g}_{i}+\tilde{h}_{i}$ where $\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{h}_{i}$ are power series with

$$ \tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}\quad,\quad\tilde{h}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}v_{j}z_{j}\text{.} $$

The first three coefficients can easily be combined via addition and subtraction i.e. $c_{j}=u_{j}\pm v_{j}$ for all $j$ . Again, this requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 2: Multiplication. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\tilde{g}_{i}\cdot\tilde{h}_{i}$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}$ and $\tilde{h}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}v_{j}z^{j}$ . Then, if $\tilde{w}_{i}=\sum_{j}c_{j}z^{j}$ , we have $c_{0}=u_{0}v_{0}$ , $c_{1}=u_{0}v_{1}+u_{1}v_{0}$ , and $c_{2}=u_{2}v_{0}+u_{1}v_{1}+u_{0}v_{2}$ . This requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 3: Division. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\tilde{g}_{i}/\tilde{h}_{i}$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}$ and $\tilde{h}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}v_{j}z^{j}$ . Since $v_{0}\neq 0$ , we obtain the inverse via ˜4.2 as

$$ \frac{1}{\tilde{h}_{i}}=\frac{1}{v_{0}}\left(1+q+q^{2}+q^{3}+\dotsc\right) $$

with $q=-\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{v_{j}}{v_{0}}z^{j}$ . In particular, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\tilde{g}_{i}}{\tilde{h}_{i}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{v_{0}}(u_{0}+u_{1}z+u_{2}z^{2}+\dots)\cdot\left(1+\left(-\frac{v_{1}}{v_{0}}z-\frac{v_{2}}{v_{0}}z^{2}-\dots\right)+\left(-\frac{v_{1}}{v_{0}}z-\dots\right)^{2}+\dots\right) \displaystyle=(u_{0}^{\prime}+u_{1}^{\prime}z+u_{2}^{\prime}z^{2}+u_{3}^{\prime}z^{3}+\dots)\cdot\left(1+\left(-v_{1}^{\prime}z-v_{2}^{\prime}z^{2}-\dots\right)+\left(-v_{1}^{\prime}z-\dots\right)^{2}+\dots\right) $$

where we set $u_{j}^{\prime}=\frac{u_{j}}{v_{0}}$ and $v_{j}^{\prime}=\frac{v_{j}}{v_{0}}$ . Finally, we have

$$ \displaystyle c_{0} \displaystyle=u_{0}^{\prime} \displaystyle c_{1} \displaystyle=u_{1}^{\prime}-u_{0}^{\prime}v_{1}^{\prime} \displaystyle c_{2} \displaystyle=u_{2}^{\prime}-u_{1}^{\prime}v_{1}^{\prime}+u_{0}^{\prime}(v_{1}^{\prime 2}-v_{2}^{\prime})\text{.} $$

This requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 4: Exponent. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\exp(\tilde{g}_{i})$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}$ . Then, using the formal power series of $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\exp(\tilde{g}_{i}) \displaystyle=\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 0}u_{j}z^{j}\right) \displaystyle=\exp(u_{0})\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 1}u_{j}z^{j}\right) \displaystyle=\exp(u_{0})\left(\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{1}{k!}\left(\sum_{j\geq 1}u_{j}z^{j}\right)^{k}\right). $$

Note that for every fixed $j\geq 0$ , there are finitely many terms in the above sum that contribute to the coefficient of $z^{j}$ , so the formal power series is well-defined. In particular,

$$ \displaystyle c_{0} \displaystyle=e^{u_{0}} \displaystyle c_{1} \displaystyle=e^{u_{0}}u_{1} \displaystyle c_{2} \displaystyle=e^{u_{0}}\left(u_{2}+\frac{u_{1}^{2}}{2}\right)\text{.} $$

This requires $O(1)$ gates. Even though the formulas use $\exp(u_{0})$ , it is a constant and can be implemented in an AC.

Case 5: Logarithm. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\ln(\tilde{g}_{i})$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j\geq 0}u_{j}z^{j}$ . Then applying the power series identity $\ln(1+x)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k+1}\frac{x^{k}}{k}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\ln(\tilde{g}_{i}) \displaystyle=\ln u_{0}+\ln\left(1+\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{u_{j}}{u_{0}}z^{j}\right) \displaystyle=\ln u_{0}+\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\cdot\left(\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{u_{j}}{u_{0}}z^{j}\right)^{k} $$

Again, for every fixed $j\geq 0$ , there are finitely many terms in the above sum that contribute to the coefficient of $z^{j}$ , so the formal power series is well-defined. In particular,

$$ \displaystyle c_{0} \displaystyle=\ln u_{0} \displaystyle c_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{u_{1}}{u_{0}} \displaystyle c_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{u_{2}}{u_{0}}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{u_{1}}{u_{0}}\right)^{2}\text{.} $$

This requires $O(1)$ gates. Similarly as the $\exp$ case, we only use $\ln$ on a constant, so it can be implemented in the AC model.

Overall, our circuit requires $O(s)$ gates to compute all the relevant coefficients. ∎

The next tool we require is the Baur-Strassen Theorem, which states that given an AC that computes a function, we can compute all the partial derivatives with a similar sized circuit.

#### Theorem 4.3 ([BS83]).

Let $F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a function and $F^{\prime}=(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{1}},\dots,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{n}})$ . If there is an AC of size $s$ computing $F$ , there is an AC of size $O(s)$ computing $F^{\prime}$ .

After Baur and Strassen [BS83] obtained this result, Morgenstern [Mor85] showed a simplified constructive proof for the Baur-Strassen theorem. Following the Morgenstern’s proof strategy, we generalize the Baur-Strassen theorem to eAC.

#### Theorem 4.4 (Extended Baur-Strassen Theorem).

Let $F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a function and let $F^{\prime}=\left\{\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{1}},\dotsc,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{n}}\right\}$ . If there is an eAC of size $s$ computing $F$ , there is an eAC of size $O(s)$ computing $F^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\left\{g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s}\right\}$ be a minimum size eAC that computes $F$ . Let $F^{(i)}$ be the function computed by $g_{i},\dotsc,g_{s}$ . Note that $F^{(i)}$ has $s-i+1$ operations and has input variables $\left\{x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n},g_{1},\dotsc,g_{i-1}\right\}$ . We prove the desired claim with induction. For notational simplicity, we define for $1\leq j\leq n+s$ , $z_{j}=x_{j}$ if $j\leq n$ and $z_{j}=g_{j-n}$ if $j>n$ . We claim that partial derivatives of $F^{(i)}$ can be computed with an eAC of size $5(s-i+1)+2$ . Then, the partial derivatives of $F=F^{(1)}$ can be computed with a circuit of size $O(s)$ .

We begin with the base case. Note $F^{(s+1)}(x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n},g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s})=g_{s}$ has partial derivatives $\frac{\partial F^{(s+1)}}{\partial g_{s}}=1$ and $\frac{\partial F^{(s+1)}}{\partial z}=0$ for any $z\in\left\{x_{i}\right\}\cup\left\{g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s-1}\right\}$ . These values are simply constants, so we can compute them using an eAC of size $1$ . While we need gates to store the two distinct values, we do not need to store all derivatives separately. In subsequent computations, we simply remember which value to use at the appropriate gate. This leads to $2$ additional gates in the computed circuit.

We now proceed with the inductive case. Assume that $\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{j}}$ is computed for all $j\leq n+i$ . Then, $F^{(i)}$ is the eAC $F^{(i+1)}$ with input $g_{i}$ substituted with some operation defined in Definition˜2.2. For any variable $z_{j}$ for $j\leq n+i-1$ , we can compute $\frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{j}}$ by the chain rule,

$$ \frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{j}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{j}}+\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial z_{j}}\text{.} $$

The case where $g_{i}$ corresponds to an operation from $\{+,-,\times,/\}$ is already handled in the Morgenstern’s proof for standard Baur-Strassen Theorem [Mor85]. Hence, we focus on the case where $g_{i}$ corresponds to an $\exp$ or $\ln$ gate.

Suppose $g_{i}$ involves input $z_{k}$ for some $k\leq n+i-1$ , and if $j\neq k$ , then $\frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{j}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{j}}$ . Hence, it suffices to compute $\frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{k}}$ .

If $g_{i}=\exp(z_{k})$ for some $k\leq n+i-1$ , we have

$$ \frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{k}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{k}}+\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}\exp(z_{k}) $$

where we have $\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{k}},\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}$ computed by induction and $\exp(z_{k})$ can be computed with one operation. Summing requires an additional operation.

Similarly, if $g_{i}=\ln(z_{k})$ , we have

$$ \frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{k}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{k}}+\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}\frac{1}{z_{k}} $$

where the above term can be computed by $3$ operations. This proves the inductive claim. ∎

Our final ingredient is a lower bound on the size of any arithmetic circuit that computes independent matrix products.

#### Lemma 4.5.

For any integer $\ell\geq 1$ , any arithmetic circuit computing $\ell$ independent $n\times n\times n$ matrix products has size $\ell\cdot n^{\omega-o(1)}$ .

Its proof follows from standard application of the asymptotic sum inequality [Sch81]. We include a proof of this lemma and necessary definitions for completeness.

A tensor $T$ over three sets of variables $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{|X|}\},Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{|Y|}\},Z=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{|Z|}\}$ is defined as

$$ T=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{ijk}x_{i}y_{j}z_{k} $$

for some coefficients $a_{ijk}\in\mathbb{R}$ . An algebraic circuit computing the tensor is an algebraic circuit that, given inputs $X,Y$ , outputs $\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}a_{ijk}x_{i}y_{j}$ for every $k\in[|Z|]$ .

The rank $R(T)$ of a tensor $T$ is defined as the smallest integer $r$ such that $T$ can be represented as

$$ \sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\alpha_{\ell,i}x_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\beta_{\ell,j}y_{j}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}\gamma_{\ell,k}z_{k}\right) $$

for some values $\alpha_{\ell,i},\beta_{\ell,j},\gamma_{\ell,k}$ . The asymptotic rank $\tilde{R}(T)$ , which is upper bounded by $R(T)$ , is defined as $\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}(R(T^{\otimes m}))^{1/m}$ , where $T^{\otimes m}$ denotes the $m$ -th tensor power of $T$ .

The matrix multiplication tensor for $n\times n\times n$ matrix products is

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{ij}y_{jk}z_{ik}\text{,} $$

and we denote it by $\langle n,n,n\rangle$ . We also denote the disjoint union of $\ell$ copies of $n\times n\times n$ as $\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle$ .

Now we are ready to state the asymptotic sum inequality.

#### Theorem 4.6 (Asymptotic Sum Inequality [Sch81]).

For integers $\ell,n\geq 1$ ,

$$ \ell\cdot n^{\omega}\leq\tilde{R}\left(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle\right). $$

We now prove Lemma˜4.5.

#### Proof of Lemma˜4.5.

Suppose there is an arithmetic circuit of size $O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ for $\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ . By definition, this circuit computes $\ell$ independent instances of $n\times n\times n$ matrix products. It is known that the rank of a tensor is at most twice the size of a circuit computing it [Str73] (see also, e.g, [Blä13, Theorem 4.7]), so $R(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle)\leq O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ , which further implies $\tilde{R}(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle)\leq O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ . Hence, by the asymptotic sum inequality [Sch81],

$$ \displaystyle\omega \displaystyle\leq\frac{\log\left(\tilde{R}(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle)/\ell\right)}{\log n} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\log\left(O(n^{\omega-\varepsilon})\right)}{\log n} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta+(\omega-\varepsilon)\log n}{\log n} \displaystyle=\omega-\varepsilon+\delta/\log n, $$

where $\delta$ is a constant depending on the constant hidden in the big- $O$ notation. As we can take $n\rightarrow\infty$ , this is a contradiction. Hence, $\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle$ does not have an arithmetic circuit of size $O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ , i.e., it has size at least $\ell\cdot n^{\omega-o(1)}$ . ∎

## 5 Lower Bounds for Large Embedding Dimension

In this section, we prove lower bounds against transformers with large embedding dimension in the extended arithmetic circuit model. Recall Theorem˜1.2:

#### Theorem 5.1 (Formal Theorem˜1.2).

There exists a transformer $T$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m=2N+3$ , $L$ layers, $H$ attention heads per layer, input dimension and output dimension $2N+3$ satisfying the following:

- 1. $T$ is computable by an eAC, each embedding is computable by an arithmetic circuit of size $O(m)$ , and all MLP maps are the identity map.

- 2. Any eAC computing $T$ has size at least $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}-O\left(LHN^{2}\right)$ .

We begin with defining a transformer that computes row sums of matrix products. First, we give a simple attention head that computes the (normalized) row sums of a single matrix product after taking entry-wise exponential. Our attention head also outputs the normalization factors, which we will later use to recover the entries of the matrix product.

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let $m\geq N$ . There is an attention unit $\mathrm{Att}_{\mathsf{MatMul}}$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m^{\prime}=\max(m+1,2N+3)$ , input dimension $2N+3$ such that for any $N\times m$ matrices $A,B$ and vector $D\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ , there exist embedding weights such that given input $X=\begin{pmatrix}Z_{1}&I_{N}&1_{N\times 1}&0_{N\times 1}\\ Z_{2}&0_{1\times N}&0&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(2N+3)}$ where $Z_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times(N+1)},Z_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times(N+1)}$ are arbitrary matrices, the output $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m^{\prime}}$ satisfies

$$ Y[i,j]=\begin{cases}\frac{N}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $j=1$}\\
\frac{D[j-1]}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
\frac{S_{i}}{1+S_{i}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $j=1$}\\
\frac{D[j-1]}{1+S_{i}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
0&\mathrm{o/w}\end{cases} $$

where $S_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(AB^{\top})_{ij}$ for $i\in[N]$ . Furthermore, all embedding maps can be computed by arithmetic circuits of size $O(Nm)$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the embeddings

$$ Q(X)=\begin{pmatrix}A&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{1\times m}&0\end{pmatrix},\quad K(X)=\begin{pmatrix}B&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{1\times m}&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(m+1)} $$

so that

1_{1\times N}&1\end{pmatrix} $$

$$ W_{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{(N+1)\times m}&0_{(N+1)\times 1}\\
A&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{2\times m}&0_{2\times 1}\end{pmatrix},\quad W_{K}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{(N+1)\times m}&0_{(N+1)\times 1}\\
B&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{2\times m}&0_{2\times 1}\end{pmatrix} $$

If $m^{\prime}>m+1$ , we can append columns of zeros to $W_{Q},W_{K}$ and therefore $Q(X),Q(K)$ without changing the value of $Q(X)K(X)^{\top}$ . Then, consider the embedding

$$ V(X)=\begin{pmatrix}1_{N\times 1}&0_{N\times 1}&0_{N\times 1}&\dots&0_{N\times 1}\\
0&D_{1}&D_{2}&\dots&D_{N}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(N+1)}\text{.} $$

$$ W_{V}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{(2N+1)\times 1}&0_{(2N+1)\times 1}&0_{(2N+1)\times(N-2)}&0_{(2N+1)\times 1}\\
1&0&0_{1\times(N-2)}&0\\
0&D_{1}&\dots&D_{N}\end{pmatrix} $$
